chunks: "A flash ADC finds the answer in a single step by checking every possible level at the same time.
You put a resistor ladder across the reference, with 2 to the N equal resistors, which gives you 2 to the N-1 evenly spaced threshold voltages.
Each threshold goes to the inverting input of its own comparator and the input signal goes to all the other inputs. If the input is, say, 1. 9 volts on a 3-bit, 3.
3 volts converter, the thresholds are 0. 41, 0. 83, 1. 24, 1. 65, and so on, so the first four comparators output high and the rest low.
That's called a thermometer code, like mercury rising. A priority encoder turns it into binary, here 100, which is 4.
The big advantage is speed: one comparator delay plus encoding, so you get giga-samples per second. The downside is cost.
An 8-bit flash needs 255 comparators and 256 resistors, and each extra bit doubles all of it: area, power, and the capacitive load on the input.
Comparator offsets also have to be much smaller than one LSB, which is hard when there are hundreds of them. So flash is limited to about 6 to 8 bits.
For higher resolution at speed people use folding, interpolating or pipelined converters, and SAR for slower, higher-resolution jobs."
